POLICE v SPICE FINANCE LTD
2026 PL3 14
IN THE DISTRICT COURT OF PORT LOUIS (DIVISION III)
Cause No.: 1032/25
Police
v/s
Spice Finance Ltd
Judgment
The accused company stands charged with the offence of « Failing to comply with the
requirements of a notice to owner » in breach of Regulations 4, 8, 11 and 12 of GN
213/04 coupled with Sections 40 and 44(2) of the Interpretation and General Clauses
Act. As per the information dated 20th January 2025, the accused company, on whom

a Notice to Owner was served on the 29th May 2019 and who at the time of the
commission of the offence, was the owner of the vehicle, to wit: private car 444 JN 13,
stands charged with having on or about the 11th June 2019, unlawfully failed to pay
the penalty within 14 days, for the offence of: « Parking vehicle on single-yellow line »
committed on the 17th April 2018 at Sir William Newton Street, Port Louis.
The accused company pleaded not guilty and was represented by its Operations
Executive.

Me Sobnack appeared for the accused company.

The case for the

Prosecution was conducted by PS Bhowon.
Case for the Prosecution
Four witnesses deponed on behalf of the Prosecution, namely PC André, the
representative of the Director of Mauritius Post Ltd, the representative of the Registrar
of Companies and PC Museligadoo.
Witness no. 1, PC André, gave evidence to the effect that on the 17th April 2018 while
he was on duty in police uniform along Sir William Newton Street, Port Louis, he saw

Page 1

 the private car bearing registration number 444 JN 13 parked on a single yellow line.
However, there was no triangular reflector placed. Witness no. 1 stated that he waited
for the driver or the owner of the vehicle but in vain and he therefore issued a PF 101B
for the offence of parking motor vehicle on single yellow line (Doc B).
Witness no. 1 was not cross-examined.
Witness no. 2, the Director of Mauritius Post Ltd, was represented by Mrs B Babna but
the latter stated that no records were available. She was briefly cross-examined and
could not confirm whether there was good service in the present matter.
Witness no. 4, the Registrar of Companies was represented by Mrs B N Emamdee,
but she was unable to confirm the details of the accused company nor whether it was
in operation at the material time. She was not cross-examined.
Witness no. 5, PC Museligadoo, gave evidence to the effect that on the 29th May 2019,
he had issued a notice to owner (Doc C). He stated that the said notice is issued to
the registered owner who is given a delay of seven days to pay the fine.
Witness no. 5 was not cross-examined.
The NLTA certificate for the vehicle bearing registration number 444 JN 13 was
produced by the Prosecution (Doc A).
Case for the Defence
No evidence was adduced on behalf of the accused company nor has its
representative made any statement in Court.

Submissions by Learned Counsel for the Accused Company
Learned Defence Counsel has submitted that in the absence of any document from
the post office, the Prosecution has failed to prove all the required element of the
offence.
The Law

Page 2

 By virtue of Regulations 8, 11 and 12 of the Road Traffic (Parking Offences)
Regulations 2004,
8. Where (a) a parking notice has been issued with respect to a vehicle under
these regulations; and
(b) the penalty has not been paid within 14 days of the date of the notice,
a traffic warden, a police officer or a road transport inspector shall serve
a notice to owner on the person who, at the time of the commission of

the offence, was the owner of the vehicle.
…
11. A person on whom a notice to owner is served may, where he is not
the owner, within 7 days after service on him of the notice, submit a
written statement to the Commissioner or Commissioner of Police, as
the case may be, giving the name and address of the person who was
the owner of the vehicle at the time of the parking offence.
12. Where the owner of a vehicle fails to pay the penalty specified in
regulation 10(c), he shall commit an offence and shall, on conviction, be
liable to a fine not less than double the penalty payable and not
exceeding 5,000 rupees.
Analysis
The presumption of innocence established by Section 10(2)(a) of the Constitution
places a burden upon the Prosecution to prove each element of the offence with which
the accused has been charged. In fact, the burden rests on the Prosecution to prove

all the elements of the offence beyond reasonable doubt1. When at the close of the
case for the Prosecution, a prima facie case has been clearly established against the
accused, the burden then shifts on him to satisfy the Court why it should not act on the
evidence adduced by the Prosecution2.

1
2

Boodhoo A. v The State [2004 SCJ 235]
Andoo M vs The Queen [1989 SCJ 257]
Page 3

 From the unchallenged contents of Doc B, I find that it has been established and
remained undisputed that on the 17th April 2018, a parking notice was issued in
respect of the vehicle bearing registration number 444 JN 13 which had been found
parked on a single-yellow line along Sir William Newton Street, Port Louis. As per Doc
B, the driver of the vehicle was required to pay a penalty of Rs 1000 within 14 days as
from the date of issue of the notice. The said driver was further informed that failing
payment of the penalty, a notice to owner will be served on the owner of the vehicle. I
find that the unchallenged contents of Doc C additionally establish that on the 29th
May 2019, witness no. 5 issued a notice to owner notifying the latter that the penalty

following the parking notice has not been paid and requesting the owner to pay the
penalty of Rs 1000 within 14 days from the date of service of the notice failing which
he will be liable to prosecution. I have found Doc B to be in the form as set out in the
First Schedule of Road Traffic (Parking Offences) Regulations 2004 and Doc C to
be in the form as set out in the Third Schedule of the said Regulations.
I note that the NLTA certificate for the vehicle bearing registration number 444 JN 13
dated 18th February 2019 (Doc A) shows the name of the owner as at that date as
Axys Leasing Ltd.

Regulation 9 of the Road Traffic (Parking Offences)

Regulations 2004 provides that:
A notice to owner shall be served by (a) delivering it to the owner; or
(b) sending it by registered post addressed to the owner at his usual or
last known place of residence or business, or any address furnished by
him.
By virtue of Section 40 of the Interpretation and General Clauses Act,

Where an enactment authorises or requires a document to be served
by post, whatever the expression used, the service shall be deemed to
be effected by properly addressing, prepaying and posting a letter
containing the document and be presumed to have been effected at the
time when the letter would be delivered in the ordinary course of post.
I find that no evidence of the relationship between the owner of the vehicle bearing
registration number 444 JN 13 as set out in Doc A and the accused company has been
adduced in the present matter. What is more, although witness no. 5 has stated that
Page 4

 he had issued the notice to owner, he did not adduce any evidence of having properly
addressed, prepaid and posted a letter containing the said notice to the registered
owner at its last known registered address. Witness no. 2 for her part, could not
confirm whether there has been good service or not in the present matter. In the
circumstances, I find that the evidence adduced by the Prosecution falls short of
establishing that the notice to owner issued by witness no. 5 in respect of the parking
notice issued by witness no. 1 was effectively served by post on the registered owner
of the vehicle bearing registration number 444 JN 13 in accordance with the provisions
of Section 40 of the Interpretation and General Clauses Act. No evidence of the

notice to owner having been otherwise delivered to the registered owner was adduced.
I consider that for the owner of a vehicle to be liable under Regulation 12 of the Road
Traffic (Parking Offences) Regulations 2004, it must be established that he has in
fact been served with the notice to owner in person or by registered post as the case
may be. This the Prosecution has however failed to establish.
Conclusion
In light of the above, I find that the Prosecution has failed to prove a material element
of the offence. The charge against the accused company is consequently dismissed.

A Dhunnoo (Miss)
District Magistrate
